title: Bearings and Oblique Triangles Checkpoint
description: Show that you can translate bearing descriptions into diagrams and identify the triangle information created by navigation situations.

questions.question: Which bearing points directly south?
questions.explanation: A 180° clockwise turn from north points south.

questions.question: A bearing of 315° lies in which quadrant?
questions.explanation: 315° is between 270° and 360°, so it lies in the northwest quadrant.

questions.question: From the same station, tower A has bearing 032° and tower B has bearing 118°. What is the angle between the sight lines?
questions.explanation: Both bearings use the same north line, so subtract: 118° - 032° = 86°.

questions.question: A ship travels 15 km from A to B on a bearing of 060°, then 10 km from B to C on a bearing of 140°. Which points form the navigation triangle?
options: The two bearings and one compass
questions.explanation: The two route legs AB and BC plus the direct distance AC form triangle ABC.

questions.question: From M to N, the bearing is 155°. What is the back bearing from N to M?
questions.explanation: Add 180° because the result stays below 360°: 155° + 180° = 335°.

questions.question: From point O, one landmark is 5 km away on bearing 010° and another is 9 km away on bearing 080°. If the distance between the landmarks is unknown, what given case is shown?
questions.explanation: The two known distances start at O, and the included angle between them is known from the bearings, so the case is SAS.

questions.question: If two bearings are measured from the same point, the smaller angle between the rays can often be found by subtracting the bearing measures.
questions.explanation: When both bearings share the same north reference, their difference gives the angle between the two rays, as long as the smaller angle is intended.

questions.question: A student draws a route from A to B and then from B to C but measures both bearings from the north line at A. Explain the error.
questions.correctAnswer: The second bearing must be measured from a north line at point B, not from the north line at A. Bearings are local directions at the point where the next leg begins.
questions.explanation: Each new turn point needs its own north reference, so the second leg should be drawn from B using a north line at B.

questions.question: A bearing of 205° tells you to draw the path in which general direction?
questions.explanation: 205° is between 180° and 270°, so the path points southwest.

questions.question: Describe the first three drawing steps for this situation: From point A, camp B is 6 km away on bearing 045°.
questions.correctAnswer: Draw point A, draw a north line through or near A, then draw ray AB 45° clockwise from north and label it 6 km.
questions.explanation: A correct bearing diagram begins with the starting point and local north line before the travel ray is measured and labeled.
